title: Base64 Feature, Matched Across Two Runs
takeaway: The base64 feature found in model A (A/1/2357) and the one found in a separately seeded model B (B/1/2165) line up on both axes the paper uses to compare features: their activations across text correlate at 0.85, and their per-vocabulary-token logit weights correlate at 0.82. The paper offers this as consistent with the two being the same feature discovered twice, not as proof of it.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Two scatter plots, each comparing one pair of features. The [[base64-feature]] A/1/2357 comes from a dictionary learning run on model A; B/1/2165 comes from a run on model B, a transformer trained on the same data with a different random seed. In both panels, run B is the horizontal axis and run A is the vertical axis, so each point is (value in B, value in A).

The left panel puts one point per token of text, at that token's feature activation in each run. The right panel puts one point per vocabulary token, at that feature's [[logit-weight]] for it — how much the feature firing pushes that token's next-token logit up or down. These are the paper's two ways of comparing features across models: [[activation-similarity]] on the left, [[logit-weight-similarity]] on the right.

### How to read it

A tight diagonal band means the two runs assign nearly the same number to the same thing. A round, untilted cloud means the two numbers are unrelated. The [[pearson-correlation]] printed above each panel summarizes the tilt: 0.85 for activations, 0.82 for logit weights.

The strips along each axis are marginal distributions, red where the token is base64-like and blue where it is not, following [[base64-proxy]]. The left panel's note applies to its axes: most probability mass sits at exactly zero, so the axis has a separate zero column before the ">0" region, and the plotted points are the rare tokens where the feature fires at all.

### What it shows

The right panel separates into two circled modes. The small red one at top right is the [[logit-weight-second-mode]] — base64-specific tokens like 'q' and 'ZX' that both features upweight. The large blue cloud near zero is labeled "Interference Weights?", the paper's guess ([[weight-interference]]) that these small weights are unwanted noise forced by [[superposition]].

Both numbers are high. Median activation correlation across all of A/1's features is 0.72 ([[feature-vs-neuron-universality]]), so 0.85 is above typical, and 0.82 is far above the Arabic pair's 0.23. Here even the interference cloud tilts diagonally; the paper does not explain that, saying only that the overlap between the two modes follows from base64 tokens also occurring in ordinary text. It reads the pair as evidence for [[universality]].

terms.definition: Feature number 2357 from dictionary learning run 1 on model A — the base64 feature the paper studies in detail. It supplies the vertical axis of both panels.
Feature number 2165 from dictionary learning run 1 on model B, the feature whose activations correlate most highly with A/1/2357. It supplies the horizontal axis of both panels.
The two separately trained one-layer transformers, each with its own sparse autoencoder run over its MLP activations. Same dataset and hyperparameters, different random seeds.
The vertical axis of the left panel: how strongly A/1/2357 fires on a given token of text. Zero means the feature is off there.
The horizontal axis of the left panel: how strongly B/1/2165 fires on the same token. Each point pairs the two runs' readings on one token.

The vertical axis of the right panel: how much A/1/2357, when active, changes the logit of one particular vocabulary token. Computed by tracing the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding.
The horizontal axis of the right panel: the same quantity for B/1/2165, for the same vocabulary token. Points are indexed by vocabulary entry, not by text position.
The subtitle of each panel: the Pearson correlation of the two coordinates plotted there. It is a summary of how tightly the cloud hugs a straight line.

The label on the small red cluster at the top right of the right panel — vocabulary tokens characteristic of base64 strings, which both features push up. These are the weights the paper takes to be the feature's deliberate effect.

The label, with the paper's own question mark, on the large blue cloud of near-zero logit weights. The suggestion is that these are cross-talk the model would set to zero if it could, not intended behavior.

Cross-talk between features whose directions in activation space are not orthogonal, so activating one slightly activates or affects others. The paper invokes it to explain the central blob rather than treating those weights as meaningful.
The hypothesis that the model packs more features than it has neurons by giving each its own direction rather than its own neuron. It is the reason the paper expects unavoidable interference weights.
The annotation under the left panel, pointing at the exact-zero column of the axis. It says the feature is inactive on the overwhelming majority of tokens, so the visible points are a small tail.
An axis marker on the left panel separating the exact-zero column from the region of small positive activations. Without the break, the zero spike would swamp the rest of the axis.

The colored bands along the left and bottom edges of each panel, showing the one-dimensional distribution of each axis on its own. Red marks base64-like tokens, blue marks the rest, following the paper's proxy coloring convention.
The thin outlines drawn around the red and blue clusters in the right panel. They mark the extent of the two modes so the reader can see them as separate populations.
The faint horizontal and vertical lines through 0.0 in the right panel. They separate tokens the feature upweights from tokens it downweights, in each run.
A text encoding that writes binary data as strings drawn from [a-zA-Z0-9+/]. It is the content both features respond to.
The paper's first cross-model comparison: treat a feature as the vector of values it takes over a fixed set of tokens, and correlate those vectors. It is what the left panel plots.
The paper's second cross-model comparison: treat a feature as the vector of logit weights it has over the vocabulary, and correlate those. It is what the right panel plots.

numbers.meaning: Pearson correlation between the two features' activations, printed above the left panel. It is high because both features fire on base64 text and stay near zero elsewhere, so their values rise and fall together token by token.

Pearson correlation between the two features' logit weight vectors, printed above the right panel. It is high partly because the shared base64 mode sits far from the origin and partly because, unusually, the central interference cloud is itself tilted along the diagonal here.

The activation range on both axes of the left panel. Feature activations are non-negative because the autoencoder's hidden layer is ReLU, and roughly 12 is the largest value either feature reaches on the sampled text.

The logit weight range on both axes of the right panel. Weights run both ways because a feature can suppress tokens as well as promote them, and the scale is small since a single feature makes a modest linear contribution to any one logit.

The origin of the logit weight axes. Softmax is shift-invariant, so logit weights have no absolute zero; the paper shifts each feature's weights so that its median weight is zero, which is what makes 0.0 a meaningful reference.
Where the red base64-token cluster sits on both logit axes. These are the tokens whose probability both features raise most when they fire.
Roughly where the blue interference cloud centers on both axes, slightly below zero. With the median pinned at zero and a positive second mode pulling upward, the bulk mode sits a little negative.

The number of tokens over which the paper computes activation correlations when searching for a feature's counterpart in the other run. It is the sample behind the 0.85 figure and behind the choice of B/1/2165 as the match.
The median activation correlation between a feature in A/1 and its best match in B/1, across all features. It is the baseline that makes 0.85 read as better than typical rather than merely nonzero.
The same median when matching transformer neurons across the two models instead of features. The paper reports it to argue that features are more consistent between models than neurons are.

The activation and logit weight correlations for the equivalent Arabic script pair earlier in the paper. The contrast matters here: the Arabic logit weights agreed only weakly because the central mode was near-isotropic noise, whereas the base64 pair reaches 0.82.
The dictionary learning run index within each model, distinguishing runs that differ in dictionary size and L1 coefficient. Both features come from run 1, so the comparison is like-for-like.
The index of each feature within its run, an arbitrary identifier assigned by training order. They carry no meaning beyond naming the two features being compared.
